title: Final: value types
cards/0/q: Counter is a mutable struct implementing ICounter with an Inc method. What does this code print?
cards/0/explain: The first cast boxes a copy of the element — the change is lost. arr[0].Inc() changes the array element itself: 1. ICounter i = arr[0] boxes a copy holding 1, i.Inc() takes the box to 2, and the element stays at 1.
cards/0/wrong/2: i is a box with a copy of the element. Changing it never reaches the array.
cards/1/q: S is a struct with no overrides that implements IDisposable and IComparable<S>. Where is there boxing, unless the JIT removes it? Select all.
cards/1/explain: GetType is an Object method, it needs an object. Equals and GetHashCode are not overridden — they go to ValueType with a box (Equals also boxes its argument). Dispose in using and CompareTo in a constrained generic are called via constrained with no box.
cards/2/q: Point is a mutable struct with an Offset method. Which line compiles but changes nothing in the data?
cards/2/explain: The List<T> indexer returns a copy: Offset changes a temporary. The array yields the element itself, with plus assignment writes a new value, and ref via AsSpan gives a reference straight into the list's internal array.
cards/3/q: struct Key { string City; int Id; } is a dictionary key, nothing overridden. Why is this bad when many keys share a city?
cards/3/options/0: The default hash comes from City only: those keys land in one bucket, and Equals goes through reflection
cards/3/options/1: Equals compares only City, so different Ids overwrite each other
cards/3/options/2: A dictionary does not accept a struct with a reference as a key
cards/3/options/3: It is fine: ValueType.GetHashCode mixes all the fields
cards/3/explain: The reference closes the fast path. The slow GetHashCode hashes the first non-null field — City. Equals still compares every field, so data does not get mixed up, but lookup becomes a walk with reflection.
cards/3/wrong/1: Equals via reflection compares every field. Keys do not get mixed up — everything is just slow.
cards/4/q: A struct key: equality with no boxes or reflection, in one line
cards/4/explain: readonly record struct generates IEquatable<Key>, Equals, GetHashCode over all fields and ==, and readonly makes the properties init — the key cannot be spoiled after insertion. A record class would give equality too, but that is a reference type with an allocation per key.
cards/5/q: Match each struct with how ValueType.Equals compares it
cards/5/pairs/4/1: Its own Equals, ValueType is not involved
cards/6/q: What does Unsafe.SizeOf<R>() return on x64?
cards/6/explain: Sequential: Kind at 0, then a 7-byte gap up to the aligned double at 8, Id at 16, 20 in total — rounded up to a multiple of 8: 24. Put the double first and the byte last, and it is 16.
cards/6/wrong/1: 13 is the sum of field sizes without alignment. You would only get that with Pack = 1.
cards/6/wrong/2: You get 16 if you reorder the fields: double, int, byte.
cards/7/q:
A HashSet

, where P is a struct without IEquatable

but with overridden Equals(object) and GetHashCode. What happens in Contains?
cards/7/options/0: No reflection, but the argument is boxed on every Equals(object) call
cards/7/options/1: No boxes and no reflection — the override is enough
cards/7/options/3: It does not compile: HashSet requires IEquatable<T>
cards/7/explain:
Without IEquatable

, EqualityComparer

.Default calls Equals(object): your own override, so no reflection, but the argument is object, which means a box per comparison. IEquatable

removes that too.
cards/7/wrong/3: HashSet works with any T: without IEquatable<T> it just falls back to Equals(object).
